records.sourceFile: Low carbohydrate availability impairs hypertrophy and anerobic performance.pdf

paper.citation: Margolis LM, Pasiakos SM. Low carbohydrate availability impairs hypertrophy and anaerobic performance. Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. 2023;26(4):347-352.
paper.abstract: This narrative review summarises mechanistic, acute and short-term studies of dietary carbohydrate restriction on muscle protein regulation, body composition, strength and anaerobic performance. The authors conclude that low-carbohydrate intake increases branched-chain amino acid oxidation and may blunt hypertrophy, while muscle strength does not appear to be impaired. They also report that low muscle glycogen impairs supramaximal exercise capacity.
paper.tldr: Carbohydrate restriction appears to increase amino acid oxidation and may blunt hypertrophy, but most of the evidence is acute or confounded by energy deficit. Strength does not appear to be reduced, and low muscle glycogen reduces high-intensity and sprint capacity.
paper.methods: Narrative review in Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care. The authors summarise acute, mechanistic and short-term studies on carbohydrate restriction and muscle protein regulation, and draw on a systematic review by Coleman et al. (13 studies, 21 to 84 days), a narrative review of glycogen and high-intensity exercise, and a systematic review of strength outcomes. No literature search method is described.
paper.findings: Acute 24-hour low-carbohydrate feeding increased branched-chain amino acid oxidation and reduced myogenic regulator transcription compared with mixed feeding. In Coleman et al., low-carbohydrate diets with exercise training produced greater losses of body and fat mass than mixed diets, and fat-free mass fell by 0.3 kg versus a gain of 0.7 kg on the mixed diet, a 1 kg difference. Across studies of 2 to 84 days, strength was not reduced, and glycogen below about 200 mmol/kg dry weight reduced time to exhaustion and repeated sprint performance.
paper.limitations: No search method or quality appraisal is described, and the review is a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic one. Most mechanistic data come from acute human studies, cell culture and mouse models, and the authors note there is no consensus on the effect of glycogen on mTORC1 signalling. Many studies did not control energy intake, so body composition changes may reflect energy deficit, and the Coleman fat-free mass difference is described by the authors as modest and heterogeneous. The Summary states that restriction impairs hypertrophy, while the body of the text says it may blunt hypertrophy. The sample size of the 8-week bodybuilder study is not given in the text.
paper.practicalImplications: The review supports advising athletes who need high-intensity exercise to avoid severe or prolonged carbohydrate restriction, because low muscle glycogen reduces supramaximal capacity. Short-term strength does not appear to be reduced by low-carbohydrate diets, but this should not be read as evidence that hypertrophy is unaffected over the long term.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The review links glycogen below about 200 mmol/kg dry weight to reduced repeated-sprint and time-to-exhaustion performance, which is relevant to sport. Strength does not appear to be impaired in studies of 2 to 84 days, but long-term effects on hypertrophy and performance are unclear.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review suggests from acute markers that low carbohydrate availability may impair muscle remodelling and repair, but it did not study injured athletes or return to sport. It cannot inform return-to-play timing, rehabilitation nutrition targets or clearance.

records.sourceFile: Making Sense of Muscle Protein Synthesis_- A Focus on Muscle Growth During Resistance Training.pdf

paper.citation: Witard OC, Bannock L, Tipton KD. Making Sense of Muscle Protein Synthesis: A Focus on Muscle Growth During Resistance Training. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2021 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This narrative review examines whether acute muscle protein synthesis responses to resistance exercise and nutrition predict chronic muscle hypertrophy during resistance training. The authors discuss physiological and methodological factors that limit this relationship and offer practical implications for practitioners.
paper.tldr: A single acute muscle protein synthesis response to exercise and protein does not reliably predict an individual's muscle growth, especially early in training. It can still help compare nutrition strategies at group level, but not by quantity.
paper.methods: A narrative review with no described search strategy. The authors evaluate studies that measured acute muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise and nutrition, mostly with stable isotope methods, and related these to hypertrophy after resistance training. They also discuss physiological factors (training status, individual variability and translational capacity) and methodological factors (timing of biopsies, the measurement method and the different definitions of hypertrophy).
paper.findings: Mitchell et al. (23 untrained young men, 16 weeks) found no correlation between myofibrillar synthesis measured over 6 hours after the first session and the change in quadriceps volume (r = .10). Mayhew et al. (36 untrained men and women, 16 weeks) found no correlation between mixed-muscle synthesis and muscle mass change. In Damas et al. (10 untrained young men, 10 weeks), synthesis at week 1 did not correlate with muscle change, whereas synthesis at week 3 correlated with change in vastus lateralis cross-sectional area (r = .9, p = .002). The authors conclude that acute synthesis responses do not predict individual hypertrophy, noting that individual responses can vary by as much as 100%, but can predict average hypertrophy at group level.
paper.limitations: The review describes no search method, so study selection cannot be checked, and it relies on a small number of studies with 10 to 36 participants. All Table 1 studies enrolled untrained participants, so the authors' practical statement that MPS 'will translate to chronic adaptations in muscle mass only in trained individuals' is not tested directly in trained athletes. The authors also note measurement limits of both synthesis and hypertrophy methods.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not use a single acute synthesis result to predict how much muscle an individual athlete will gain. The authors suggest acute synthesis studies remain useful as a starting point for comparing protein sources and interventions at group level, with expectations managed because some athletes will not respond. Quantitative differences in synthesis should not be converted into predicted differences in hypertrophy.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete programming, the review supports treating acute protein-synthesis findings as a starting point for trying a nutrition or training strategy, with the individual athlete's response checked over time. It does not support using these findings as a guarantee of muscle gain.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport. Its material on muscle damage concerns healthy adults after unaccustomed eccentric exercise, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Meldonium supplementation in professional athletes - Career destroyer or lifesaver.pdf

paper.citation: Pușcaș A, Buț MG, Vari CE, Ősz BE, Ștefănescu R, Filip C, et al. Meldonium supplementation in professional athletes: career destroyer or lifesaver? Cureus. 2024;16(7):e63634.
paper.abstract: The authors describe meldonium's proposed effects on carnitine metabolism, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress and inflammation. They discuss whether these effects could protect the heart of athletes, while noting that meldonium is on the WADA prohibited list.
paper.tldr: Meldonium is banned for competing athletes, and its proposed mechanisms, such as reduced fatty acid oxidation and less oxidative stress, come mostly from animal and cell studies. The review does not show improved endurance or heart health in athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of animal, cell and clinical literature on meldonium, with no search method reported. The authors describe its carnitine-related mechanisms, its effects in animal models of mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation, and its use in cardiac patients.
paper.findings: Meldonium inhibits the enzyme that makes carnitine and shifts fatty acid oxidation toward peroxisomes, which the authors propose reduces acyl-carnitine build-up and oxidative stress. In animal models it reduced mitochondrial DNA damage, oxidative stress and inflammation, including in a rat sepsis model. The human evidence cited comes from trials in patients with heart failure and in a phase 2 trial of 512 patients with stable angina, where exercise tolerance improved in a dose-dependent way, and the authors state that few human studies link meldonium to sports performance.
paper.limitations: The review gives no search or appraisal method, and most mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cell and fish studies. The cited human trials are in heart failure and angina patients rather than athletes, and no athlete performance or cardiac data are reported. The authors' claims that meldonium improves endurance and that no negative effects have been shown in athletes are not supported by data presented in the review.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should treat meldonium as a WADA-listed prohibited metabolic modulator (S4 list since 2016) and confirm its current status before advising any athlete. It should not be presented as a cardioprotective supplement, because the review's support for that is mechanistic, animal-based or from cardiac patients. The review notes that athletic heart changes can be hard to distinguish from cardiomyopathy, which is a reason for clinical assessment rather than self-treatment.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff should not plan around meldonium as an endurance or recovery aid, because the performance claims rest on mechanistic and animal evidence and the substance is prohibited in competition.
paper.rtp: The review concerns the metabolic and cardiac mechanisms of a prohibited substance and does not evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport after injury or illness. It should not be used to decide when an athlete can return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: Methodologies for Investigating        Performance Changes With Supplement Use.pdf

paper.citation: Burke LM, Peeling P. Methodologies for Investigating Performance Changes With Supplement Use. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018.
paper.abstract: This scholarly review sets out how performance supplement studies should be designed, controlled and interpreted so that claims about sports performance can be tested. It covers crossover and parallel designs, blinding, confounding variables, combined and repeated supplement use, and whether small changes are meaningful in competition.
paper.tldr: Supplement studies need well-trained athletes, reliable performance tests, good controls and realistic protocols before their results can guide practice. Combined and repeated supplement use have been poorly studied.
paper.methods: Narrative scholarly review. The authors discuss design options (crossover, parallel, stratified and matched allocation), blinding and presentation of treatments, confounding variables, and interpretation of individual responses and small performance changes, with examples from several supplements. No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors state that the supplement evidence base is limited by small samples, weak methods and few studies of combined or repeated use. They note that crossover designs need fewer athletes but may need washout periods. They recommend reporting percentage change with 90 to 95% confidence limits and a smallest worthwhile change, warn that apparent individual responses are often confused with day-to-day variability, and note that gains of about 0.5 to 1% may matter in competition.
paper.limitations: The authors describe the review as brief and acknowledge that many supplement studies are small and of limited quality. The examples are illustrative rather than a systematic synthesis.
paper.practicalImplications: When judging a supplement study, check whether it used well-trained athletes, a reliable performance test, a placebo and a protocol that matches the event, and whether claims about responders account for normal day-to-day variability. The review also notes that combined and repeated use are poorly studied, so benefits seen with a single use may not carry over.
paper.athleteDev: Before a supplement is added to a program, check whether the evidence used a test that matches the event and whether any claimed individual responses were confirmed with repeated trials. The review does not show that any particular supplement improves performance.
paper.rtp: This review concerns performance supplements in competition and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Navigating the Risks Beyond the Label - Unpacking Global Nutritional Supplement Safety.pdf

paper.citation: Wardenaar FC, Burns SF, Campos M, Chan Y, Claassen-Smithers A, Dunshea-Mooij C, et al. Navigating the Risks Beyond the Label: Unpacking Global Nutritional Supplement Safety. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2025 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Global overview of nutritional supplement use among athletes, relevant authorities, legislation and safety measures, with a focus on third-party testing (TPT). Data were drawn from peer-reviewed studies, government sources and regional expert contributions across six world regions. Reported use ranged from 7% to 100%, higher-risk products such as herbal blends, preworkouts and weight-management products were reported in all regions, and TPT was concentrated in Europe, North America and Australia/New Zealand.
paper.tldr: Supplement use among athletes is widespread, and products such as preworkouts, herbal blends and weight-loss products carry a higher risk of banned substances in every region. Third-party tested products are concentrated in a few countries, so athletes in other regions face greater anti-doping and health risks.
paper.methods: Scholarly review with six regional sections written by two to three co-authors per region, combining desk research with local performance nutrition input. Co-authors listed relevant studies from PubMed and Google Scholar, preferring studies from 2014 to 2025 of elite adult athletes, and classified athlete tiers using the McKay et al. framework. The authors also listed national authorities, legislation and TPT programs, and included anecdotes from stakeholders. No systematic search protocol, screening or quality appraisal is reported.
paper.findings: Reported supplement use ranged from 7% (Nepal national athletes) to 100% (several studies), with protein, multivitamins, creatine, caffeine and sports drinks most common. The authors cite analytical studies in which 14% to 50% of tested supplements were positive for prohibited substances, and a Duiven et al. study in which at least one in five supplements contained ingredients not on the label. TPT use among athletes was reported at 18% to 85%, mostly in Western countries. The text also cites an estimate that about 9% of US doping cases involved nutritional supplements.
paper.limitations: The review acknowledges that studies on supplement use lack methodological standardization, differ in recall period and assessment method, and that TPT use data come mainly from Western countries. The anecdotes are described by the authors as subjective and drawn from memory, and several authors disclose supplement-industry ties, including one author employed by a company that sells dietary supplements. Recommendations, such as a food-first approach and harmonized TPT standards, are author consensus rather than tested interventions.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should ask athletes to check whether any product they use is third-party tested for banned substances, and to record the batch or lot number. Preworkouts, fat burners, herbal blends and products bought from unregulated sources or compounding pharmacies should be treated as higher risk, and athletes should be warned that supplements may contain ingredients not listed on the label.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports choosing supplements through a team policy and a food-first approach, with TPT products where a supplement is needed. Performance benefits are not assessed in the review, so the choice of supplement should rest on evidence for the specific purpose and on anti-doping risk.
paper.rtp: The review does not address rehabilitation or return to sport. Its concern with contaminated and undeclared ingredients is relevant to medications and recovery products used after injury, so medical staff should check any product used during rehabilitation against the anti-doping rules.
